questions.text: The stack needs a vent to the outside: up through the roof from the attic shaft (a new roof outlet), or an air admittance valve in the shaft if the installer allows it (usually the drain still needs one open vent above the roof somewhere).
Where is the existing stack? The proposal is a new one, straight up the void beside the hall cupboard; the old one is taken out where it is found.
The hatch in the old washing-machine corner shows a crawl space there. Does it run under the whole ground floor, including the old garage (guest room)? How deep is it?
Where is the sewer connection (the inspection point at the front)? Is rain water separate?
Attic shower (note 42): the installer to confirm the low drain's build height (about 67 mm) and the 40 mm step into the shower, or a slightly different raise for the drain they pick.

Noise: the check puts the unit at about 37 dB(A) at full power in no. 10's garden (40 allowed at night, 45 by day with the night limit on), judged 1.5 m above the ground because the annexes screen it. That holds only if no. 10 has no living-room window looking onto our garage roof (a roof light, a dormer, a window in their gable): there it is judged on the boundary 1.5 m above our roof, about 59 dB(A), too loud in every mode. Is no. 10 built like ours, mirrored? The installer confirms it with the government's tool (with a 3 dB margin: mode 4 at night, or the night limit).
Can the annex's flat roof take the outdoor unit (78 kg plus tiles, about 150 kg on 0.75 m²)? What is under the roofing over the ground-floor bathroom: timber joists or concrete?
Wall heating: wanted anywhere, besides the floor heating (floorheating.py)?

The meter cupboard is the hall cupboard by the front door (the owners): is there room in its group box for two new 16 A groups (outdoor and indoor unit)? The cables' route from it to the laundry is still open (the crawl space can be reached from the cupboard).
Thermostat: an OpenTherm thermostat in the living room, wired to the indoor unit. Where?
System volume: the Blackbird wants about 60 L in the heating circuit (a buffer tank, or 3-4 floor heating groups always open with their pump on the indoor unit's output). Which?
The outdoor unit's 1 m protection zone must stay free of ventilation openings: keep the ground floor's ventilation (its roof outlets over the laundry) and any roof light at least 1 m away.

Upstairs a new screed on insulation (the owners): the model fits it into the 70 mm assumed above the slab, a thin system (about 25 mm boards, the pipes, 30 mm of screed). A standard heating screed with its insulation needs 90-100 mm: may the first floor's and the attic's floors rise 2-3 cm?
The heat-loss calculation (ISSO 51) decides the spacing (the model: 100 mm downstairs, 150 mm upstairs) at the heat pump's 35 °C, and whether some rooms need more (wall heating).

Manifolds: the laundry's (behind the curtain), a cabinet low on the stair foot's south wall, and recessed into the landings' walls upstairs (the first floor's takes 6 cm off the back of the walk-in wardrobe's east unit, the attic's off the storage room's west cupboard). The stair foot's could be recessed too if its 100 mm wall is thickened. The first floor's feed rises in a boxing in the corridor's corner north of the washbasin niche.
Control: a thermostat per room with actuators on the manifolds, or a few zones (a heat pump runs best with most loops open)?

Bathrooms: a mat each (about 250, 380 and 200 W, showers included) with a thermostat, and the first floor's heated wall (about 200 W) with its own controller: a timer, or a thermostat? Each bathroom wants a group with a 30 mA RCD.
Unheated apart from the leads crossing them: the master bedroom's bay by the side window. Enough?

Where is the water meter, and where does the water company's pipe come in? The model assumes the meter cupboard in the hall (low on its south wall; the floor heating's manifold takes the east wall) and takes the main from there under the floor to the laundry.

Circulation, yes or no? The hot main up to the attic holds about 4 L. Without circulation the attic basin waits about 48 s for hot water and the attic shower 37 s (4.8 and 5.5 L, over the 3 L rule of thumb). The model has a circulation loop to the attic (a pump on a timer: a few seconds' wait everywhere). It keeps 25 m of pipe warm, roughly 150 W while it runs (the heat pump makes most of it), and as the Weheat tank has no circulation connection the return enters its cold inlet, which stirs the cold bottom of the tank and costs the heat pump some efficiency. Alternatives: no circulation and accept the wait, or no circulation with an electric trace heater on the hot riser.

First-floor shower: it hangs on the gable itself (Formae's update), so its two pipes leave the pipe box at the glass and run 0.4 and 0.55 m sideways in chases in the gable's inner leaf to the thermostat, the way the old bath's mixer was fed. Horizontal chases in a load-bearing masonry leaf need the constructor's OK (the Eurocode allows only vertical ones without a calculation in a 100 mm leaf): may they? Otherwise the pipes come down from the lowered ceiling in vertical chases.

First-floor basin: a concealed wall mixer needs about 80-100 mm of wall; the west wall behind the basin is 60 mm. Build it out (a 20-40 mm lining behind the basin), or a mixer with its body on the wall?
Outside taps: one in the garden (frost-free, by the kitchen's back wall) and one at the front for the drive? Anything else in the kitchen (a boiling-water tap, a fridge with water)?

The first-floor bathroom's old extract: its valve 130 cm from the window wall, 65 cm from the gable, the duct straight up through the attic and the roof (the owners, 2026-10-15). Is the duct Ø125, and is there a fan on the roof or is it a passive vent?
The kitchen's old ceiling valve and its duct cast in the roof slab: where does it run, how big is it (camera)? The old toilet's valve joins the same duct in the slab (the owners, 2026-10-15).
The annex roof's two old pipes (the old garage's vent, the old MV box's exhaust): their size (Ø125 assumed) and condition (camera).

The garage opening gets a new window (Formae): ask the window maker for HR++ glass with a laser-structured (RF-transparent) coating. Ordinary HR++ blocks WiFi about as much as the brick; with it the guest room's access point would reach the car on the drive on 5 GHz too, not only 2.4. The same goes for the kitchen's back windows if they are replaced.
The doorbell sits on the 8 cm of brick between the door frame and the downpipe. If that's too tight, it goes just right of the downpipe, or the downpipe moves a few centimetres.

Products: the proposal is Daikin (Stylish wall units, quiet; a 4-room multi-split for upstairs and a 2-room one for the ground floor). Is Daikin fine, or does Art's installer prefer another make (Mitsubishi, Panasonic)? One 6-room outdoor unit instead of two is possible but larger, louder and its R32 charge is higher.

The outdoor units: on the annex roof west of the heat pump, backs to the house wall, blowing east, in front of the stair's glass-block window. OK? They blow towards the heat pump 1.15 m away: in winter an AC heating a room would blow cold air at its intake (rarely, with the floor heating on). Their noise at no. 10's boundary (about 2.6 m) is near the Bbl's 40 dB(A): the installer calculates it; night-quiet mode or a screen may be needed.

Child's room (with the ventilation's option A3, 2026-10-12): the unit on the alcove's north wall, blowing south down the room (the bed in the south-east corner out of its path), its lines through the box's north part and the north eaves (option L3) and its condensate pumped into the eaves to the downpipe: a mini pump in the child's room (about 20 dB(A) while it runs, only when cooling). OK, or a quieter pump model / the unit somewhere with a falling drain?

Child's room and study (the owners, 2026-10-13, option L3): their lines go up into the north eaves (two core drills in the attic floor), out through the gable (two through the 350 mm wall) and down its outside in a cover about 2.5 m tall onto the annex roof, then in a duct along the wall to the outdoor unit, so no line set crosses a flat duct and the lowered ceilings stay 12 cm. The cover's colour and the holes: OK for Formae and the structural engineer?

Ground floor: the lines go through the crawl space and up the guest room / bathroom wall (the ground-floor shower's back wall: does its mixer go on another wall?). Does the crawl space reach under the old garage, and can the lines pass under the load-bearing wall (a hole through its foundation)?

Attic (built a few years later): the upstairs outdoor unit is bought for four rooms now, the attic's port capped; its lines are laid through the first floor now (capped) so the finished bathroom needn't be opened later. Or a separate small outdoor unit for the attic when it is built (a third unit on the roof: more noise)? Its condensate goes into the attic shower's drain.
Power: two new 16 A groups in the meter cupboard (one per outdoor unit), next to the heat pump's two. Is there room in the group box?

issues.text: House drain: kitchen to the street: passes under the load-bearing wall's foundation: needs a sleeve through it
issues.why: In the crawl space the pipe crosses under a wall, where the wall stands on its foundation beam. It can't be cast in: it goes through a sleeve (a larger pipe round it, a 'mantelbuis') in or under the beam, so the pipe can be pulled out and the beam can settle without crushing it. A hole in the beam needs the structural engineer's OK; the existing pipes may already have sleeves to reuse.

issues.text: Outdoor units together at the boundary with no. 10 (beyond the annex): about 38 dB(A) all at full power, the AC units in night-quiet mode 27; 40 allowed (rule of thumb)
issues.why: The rules (Bbl art. 4.107) allow an outdoor heat pump or AC unit 40 dB(A) at the boundary with a neighbour's plot in the evening and at night, 45 by day if it has its own night setting. A unit on a roof is judged on the boundary 1.5 m above the roof, or 1.5 m above the ground when the neighbour's garden and their living rooms' windows stay under the limit. This is an estimate from the unit's maximum sound power, with the houses screening it; units running together add up. A lower mode, a night limit, a screen or another place lowers it; the installer makes the real calculation (the government's tool, with a 3 dB margin).
